headline: 2026 House midterm election results as Democrats capture majority with major wins
author: Caitlin Yilek

paragraphs.text: House election results for the 2026 midterms:

• Democrats won control of the House in the 2026 midterm elections, CBS News projects, with victories in battleground districts across the country. The decisive wins came as President Trump's approval rating hit 38%, historically low for a president in the midterms, in an election where 89% of voters said cost of living was a major or crucial factor in their votes.

• GOP House Speaker Mike Johnson announced in a call with his staff Wednesday that he will not run for minority leader when the new Congress is seated. Reps. Jim Jordan and Steve Scalise told Republicans they want the job.

• Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader, said he expects his party to win at least 255 seats after all the votes are counted. He also said no one in the caucus has raised the idea of impeaching President Trump. "We've been relentlessly focused on affordability and on accountability," he told reporters.

• All 435 seats in the House of Representatives were up for election. Democrats, who had 214 seats going into the midterms, flipped more than 40 GOP-held seats and proved to be competitive in battlegrounds and in some unexpected places.

• Democrats won in battleground districts nationwide, in North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Texas, Michigan, New York, Ohio, Kentucky and Colorado, among other states. Several races still remain to be called, two days after the election.
• Republicans in several states, including Texas and Florida, had redistricted to try to gain an edge in the elections, but redrawing ultimately did not stave off their losses.
Democrats flip outgoing GOP Rep. Nancy Mace's South Carolina district
Democrat Nancy Lacore beat Republican Jenny Costa Honeycutt in South Carolina's 1st District, CBS News projected.
The seat is currently held by GOP Rep. Nancy Mace, who lost her primary earlier this year for South Carolina governor.
Lacore, a former Navy admiral, was fired during Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's tenure.

Republican Mark Lamb wins Arizona's 5th District seat
Republican Mark Lamb won his race for Arizona's 5th District against Democrat Elizabeth Lee. The seat was left open by GOP Rep. Andy Biggs' decision to run for governor.

Gluesenkamp Perez wins competitive Washington race
Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez won a third term in Washington's 3rd Congressional District, CBS News projected.
Gluesenkamp Perez's victory, in a district President Trump has won three times, comes as she's flexed her independence over party loyalty.

The congresswoman beat Republican state Sen. John Braun to win reelection in the rural district in the southwestern corner of the state. Braun, the top Republican in the Washington state Senate, was a more mainstream Republican than Gluesenkamp Perez's prior opponent, far-right conservative Joe Kent, who went on to become Mr. Trump's counterterrorism chief before resigning in protest over the Iran war. But Braun, who was endorsed by Mr. Trump, also distanced himself from the president on some issues, including tariffs, the Iran war and affirming that Joe Biden won the 2020 election.

Democrat Amish Shah beat Republican Jay Feely in Arizona's 1st District, CBS News projected.
The seat is currently held by eight-term GOP Rep. David Schweikert, who ran unsuccessfully for governor.
Shah's primary win in July was part of a string of high-profile defeats for the national Democratic Party, which backed his opponent, Republican-turned-Democrat Marlene Galán-Woods.
Shah, a physician and former state legislator, was the party's nominee in 2024.

Feely, an NFL veteran and former analyst for CBS Sports, initially ran in Arizona's 5th District, but President Trump endorsed one of Feely's primary opponents and urged him to run in a different district or for another office.

Joe Neguse announces bid for Democratic leadership post
Democratic Rep. Joe Neguse of Colorado announced his bid for assistant speaker when Democrats take over the House majority.

"With our decisive and overwhelming victory this week, it is more important than ever for the House Democratic Caucus to be unified in the 120th Congress, and to repay the faith that the American people have put in us to lower costs, end corruption, and deliver for working families. To that end, and as we embark on that road together, I write to respectfully request your support for Assistant Speaker," he wrote in a letter to his Democratic colleagues on Thursday.

"If elected Assistant Speaker, my goals would be straight-forward — to prioritize direct member services for every member of our diverse and talented caucus, and to assist Speaker Jeffries and our incredible Democratic Leadership team," he said.

The leadership hierarchy could be a point of tension as both Neguse and Rep. Ted Lieu of California seek to claim the No. 4 spot. Neguse currently holds the No. 5 spot in the minority as assistant Democratic leader. A source familiar with the matter told CBS News that assistant speaker is the No. 4 spot in the majority.

Lieu, who currently holds the No. 4 spot in the minority as Democratic Caucus vice chair, will run for Caucus chair. A source familiar with the matter told CBS News that the leadership hierarchy will be the same as it is now — with Lieu as No. 4 and Neguse as No. 5.

Top Democrat on House Oversight Committee lays out investigative agenda
Rep. Robert Garcia of California, who will be the chairman of the House Oversight Committee next Congress, laid out four areas where the panel will focus its investigative efforts.

The overarching investigations include the Trump family's business dealings, corporate corruption, actions of the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the Jeffrey Epstein scandal.

"I think folks that need to be concerned first are administration officials that have caused real harm. We're going to investigate the abuses," Garcia said at a news conference in his district on Wednesday.
Garcia singled out Stephen Miller, Corey Lewandowski and Kristi Noem, as well as members of the Trump family.
"There's a lot of folks that need to understand that we are going to ask them to testify in front of the U.S. Congress," Garcia said.

Garcia acknowledged that the Justice Department under the Trump administration is unlikely to enforce any consequences for those who do not cooperate with the panel's investigations. But he said that in the majority, Democrats will have the power to sue on behalf of the House.
"And secondly, we have the power of contempt charges. And contempt charges not only go to the DOJ, there's also a civil contempt process that goes to the courts," he said.

Asked about the potential for Democrat-led investigations, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said: "As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."

Jeffries officially announces he's running for House speaker
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries officially announced his candidacy for House speaker next Congress in a letter to the Democratic caucus on Wednesday.

"Congratulations on your election to the 120th Congress. I write to humbly request your support in connection with my candidacy to serve as the next Speaker of the House of Representatives," he wrote.

Jeffries laid out his immediate priorities, including reversing cuts to Medicaid and SNAP that were enacted as part of President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, extending the Affordable Care Act premium tax credits that expired last year, ending the Iran war and rolling back the president's tariffs.
"House Democrats must do everything in our power to meaningfully lower the high cost of living. In doing so, we will try to find bipartisan common ground whenever and wherever possible," he said.
House members from both parties will elect a speaker in early January — an election that is widely expected to favor Jeffries given Democrats' large majority.

California has nonpartisan top-two primaries, allowing two members of the same party to advance to the general election if they are the top vote getters.

The House Ethics Committee was investigating sexual misconduct allegations against Gomez, including that he engaged "in inappropriate sexual contact with a House staffer." Gomez acknowledged that he "made personal mistakes outside my marriage" and that his "actions were consensual in nature."

Progressive William Lawrence beats GOP Rep. Tom Barrett in key Michigan district
Progressive William Lawrence beat one-term Republican Rep. Tom Barrett in Michigan's 7th Congressional District, CBS News projected.

Lawrence, a climate activist who co-founded the Sunrise Movement and is a former member of the Democratic Socialists of America, defeated two moderate candidates who split the vote in the Democratic primary.

Republican David Valadao, who voted for Trump's impeachment, loses reelection in California
GOP Rep. David Valadao lost his reelection bid in California's 22nd District, CBS News projected.

Valadao's loss against Democrat Randy Villegas makes him the last of the House Republicans who voted to impeach President Trump over the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol to lose reelection or announce their retirement.

Valadao was first elected in 2012, but lost in 2018 when Democrats flipped more than 40 seats and won back control of the House. He won the seat back from Democrats in 2020, and went on to become one of the 10 House Republicans who voted to impeach Mr. Trump. Only two remain in Congress — Valadao and Rep. Dan Newhouse of Washington, who is retiring.

Scalise running for minority leader, says GOP "will need to be honest with ourselves about what happened"

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise announced he also intends to run for minority leader, telling GOP colleagues in a five-page letter that the election outcome "was far worse than any of us expected."

"This is no doubt a challenging time for our conference, but overcoming adversity is nothing new to me. Jeffries: "I haven't had a single member of the House Democratic Caucus talk to me about impeachment"
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said no one in the Democratic Caucus has raised impeaching President Trump with him.
"I haven't had a single member of the House Democratic Caucus talk to me about impeachment," Jeffries said Wednesday. "We've been relentlessly focused on affordability and on accountability."
Though Mr. Trump has warned that he's expecting Democrats to impeach him, few are eager to go through the process again.

"I think our responsibility is to focus on issues and legislation that could make a material difference in working people's lives right now," Rep.-elect Melat Kiros, a Colorado Democrat, told CBS News in a recent interview. "I'm not convinced that there is a path forward for impeaching the president that would lead to removal. And if we don't have a hope for removal, I think our time would be better spent focusing on legislation that we could actually pass that could support working families in this moment."

Hakeem Jeffries: "We will win at least 255 seats"
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries expects Democrats to win at least 255 seats, once the outcomes of all the remaining races are determined.

"Mike Johnson was correct. The polls were wrong. It wasn't simply a blue wave. It was an American tsunami," the New York Democrat said Wednesday at a news conference in Washington, D.C. "We will win at least 255 seats, if not more."
"It's a historic majority in the 21st century," he said.

Rep. Suzane DelBene of Washington, who is the chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said, "Our victory is not just impressive because of how many seats we gained — although we did gain a lot — what was incredible about last night was how far we reached into deep-red territory."
The largest majority held by either party was in the 111th Congress in 2009, when Democrats held 257 seats.

The president's party typically loses House seats in midterm election

Midterm elections are typically rough for the sitting president's party — when members of Congress lack the allure of a presidential candidate atop the ballot to galvanize voter turnout. Members of the president's party also have to reckon with their leader's sinking approval ratings and the subsequent voter backlash.
Since 1934, there have been just three instances in which the sitting president's party has gained House seats in non-presidential election years, according to the American Presidency Project.

The last time was in 2002, when President George W. Bush had a strong approval rating after the 9/11 terrorist attacks and Republicans added eight seats to their majority. Democrats gained four seats in 1998 when Bill Clinton was in office, though Republicans still retained the majority. Democrats added nine seats to their majority in 1934 during Franklin D. Roosevelt's presidency.
